**First Studio Ghibli film to win the Japan Academy Film Prize for Picture of the Year** | Year of Award | Winning Film | Release Year | |---------------|--------------|--------------| | **1998** | *Princess Mononoke* (Japanese title: *Mononoke Hime*) | 1997 | *Princess Mononoke* was the first Ghibli feature to capture the top honor at the Japan Academy Film Prize (the Japanese equivalent of the Oscars). While it had already earned the award for Best Animation in 1998, it also took home the coveted “Picture of the Year” trophy that same year—an unprecedented achievement for an animated film in Japan’s mainstream awards circuit. --- ### How its box‑office success boosted Ghibli’s international popularity | Domestic impact | International impact | |-----------------|----------------------| | • Grossed **¥1.5 billion** (≈ US$12 million) in Japan, making it the highest‑grossing Ghibli film at the time.
• Became the most‑watched Japanese film of 1997, cementing Miyazaki’s status as a national icon. | • Distributed worldwide by **Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures** (under the title *Princess Mononoke*), giving the studio a high‑profile platform in North America.
• Earned **$1.9 million** in the U.S. and Canada, a record for a foreign‑language animation at the time.
• Sparked a wave of interest in Ghibli’s catalogue among Western audiences, leading to subsequent releases of *My Neighbor Totoro*, *Kiki’s Delivery Service*, and *Spirited Away* in the U.S. and Europe. | | • The film’s critical acclaim (including a nomination for the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature in 1999) further validated Ghibli’s artistic credibility on the world stage. | • Established a template for future co‑distribution deals (e.g., Disney’s partnership with Ghibli for *Spirited Away* and *Howl’s Moving Castle*).
• Helped secure licensing agreements for merchandise, video games, and theme park attractions abroad. | | • The success prompted the studio to pursue more ambitious projects, such as *Princess Mononoke*’s sequel *Princess Mononoke: The Sacred Forest* (planned but never realized). | • Contributed to the rise of “anime” as a mainstream genre in the West, paving the way for streaming platforms (Netflix, Amazon Prime) to acquire Ghibli titles in the 2010s. | In short, *Princess Mononoke*’s domestic box‑office triumph proved that Ghibli could produce commercially viable, critically acclaimed cinema. Its international release—backed by Disney’s marketing muscle—introduced Western audiences to the studio’s distinct blend of environmental storytelling, complex characters, and lush hand‑painted visuals. This breakthrough laid the groundwork for Ghibli’s later global successes, most notably *Spirited Away*’s 2003 Oscar win and the worldwide cult following that followed.
